about: The stops and attractions framing the 1925 streetcar map: one box each, numbered clockwise from the top left. Each note is written from the sources listed with it; `at` is the point the box is centred on, `line` the car line that served it in 1925.

stops.title: Westhampton Park
stops.note: The streetcar company opened an amusement park by the lake in May 1902, with a small copy of the Eiffel Tower. It never paid: the morning cars stopped in 1907, and Richmond College bought the land in 1910. By 1914 its new campus stood where the rides had been.

stops.title: State Fair Grounds
stops.note: The State Fair came back in 1906 on a triangle of ground at the top of the Boulevard, and opened with an airshow. Its exhibition hall of 1908 later became the Richmond Arena, and races ran on its track. The fair moved out in 1941; The Diamond stands here now.

stops.title: Ginter Park
stops.line: Lakeside line and the Ashland interurban
stops.note: Lewis Ginter, the cigarette millionaire, began buying Northside land in the late 1880s. Ginter Park was among Richmond's first streetcar suburbs. Cars up Chamberlayne Avenue ran on past it to his Lakeside Park, just beyond the top of this map, with its lake, zoo and nine-hole golf course.

stops.title: Barton Heights
stops.line: Lakeside line, over the First Street viaduct
stops.note: James Barton sold lots on easy terms and had a viaduct built across Bacon's Quarter Branch, so a car could run every 20 minutes to Broad Street. Begun in 1894, it was one of the country's first trolley suburbs: a Henrico town from 1896, and part of Richmond from 1914.

stops.title: Highland Park
stops.line: Highland Park line, over the Fifth Street viaduct
stops.note: Cars crossed the Northside Viaduct and turned round a loop at the top of the hill. Advertisements promised the newly annexed suburb fresh air and less than 15 minutes by trolley to Seventh and Broad. Its line, run through to Hull Street, was Richmond's last: the final car ran on 25 November 1949.

stops.title: Nine Mile Road
stops.line: Venable Street line, toward Seven Pines
stops.note: The Richmond City and Seven Pines Railway laid track out the old New Bridge Road in 1888 and electrified it in 1892, two years after Highland Springs was founded along it. In 1918 the federal government bought the line to carry workers to a wartime powder-bagging plant.

stops.title: Church Hill and Jefferson Park
stops.line: Marshall Street and Jefferson Avenue lines
stops.note: The hill holds the city's original plat. From 1911, cars reached it across Shockoe Valley on the Marshall Street Viaduct. In October 1925 the railroad tunnel under Jefferson Park caved in during repairs, killing at least three men; their bodies are still inside.

stops.title: Seventh and Broad
stops.note: Frank Sprague put $75,000 of his own into finishing the Clay Street line in May 1888, the first big electric street railway that worked. By 1925 the lines all met downtown, and Seventh and Broad was the corner suburbs measured themselves by.

stops.title: Manchester
stops.line: Hull Street line, over the Mayo Bridge
stops.note: An independent city until it joined Richmond in 1910, when Richmond promised a better Mayo Bridge. The arched concrete bridge of 1913 carried streetcars from 14th Street onto Hull Street, Manchester's main street of shops, restaurants and theatres.

stops.title: Woodland Heights
stops.line: Forest Hill line, down Semmes Avenue
stops.note: The Southside Land and Improvement Company bought the old Rhodes place in 1889 and sold off lots east and north of it. A streetcar line opened in 1890 to serve the new suburb, running down the middle of Semmes Avenue to the park at its end.

stops.title: Forest Hill Park
stops.line: Forest Hill line, end of the line
stops.note: The favourite trolley park of all: an amusement park at the end of the line from 1890, with a boat lake, a bath house and the Dip-the-Dips roller coaster. The coaster was condemned in 1931 and the rides came down in 1932. The city bought the 105 acres in 1934.

stops.title: Byrd Park
stops.note: Laid out from 1874 around the city's new reservoir, Reservoir Park took William Byrd's name by 1907 and added lakes over the next decade. Next door, the Idlewood amusement park opened in 1906 at the end of the car line, with a horse-show pavilion and lit lagoons. It was gone by 1914.

stops.title: The Fan
stops.line: Main Street, Floyd Avenue and Broad Street lines
stops.note: Houses filled the blocks between the car lines on Main Street, Floyd Avenue and Broad Street, one of Richmond's first streetcar suburbs. The city's 1906 annexation came, as one historian puts it, "in direct response to the trolley." Floyd Avenue cars ran on west to Westhampton.

stops.title: Broad and Laurel
stops.note: The interurban's terminal. Big, fast electric cars ran to Lakeside from July 1907 and on to Ashland, crossing Bacon's Quarter Branch on a half-mile concrete trestle. Reorganized as the Richmond–Ashland Railway, the line lasted until 1938. The terminal building still stands.
